papers.title: Modelling vortex interactions reveals distinct patterns of brain reconfiguration following psilocybin and escitalopram
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder is a leading cause of disability, yet how interventions reorganise brain dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how psilocybin and escitalopram reshape brain dynamics in depression using pre- and post-treatment resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) from a double-blind randomised controlled trial (NCT03429075). We compared two whole-brain modelling approaches: conventional signal-space modelling describing interactions between regional brain signals, and vortex-space modelling capturing interactions between evolving patterns of local synchronisation. This represents the first application of vortex-space modelling to a psychiatric disorder. Vortex space was more sensitive than signal space in most analyses, including distinguishing treatment-related brain states, relating baseline connectivity to clinical improvement and predicting response to escitalopram. Our results further revealed distinct patterns of reorganisation following the two interventions. Psilocybin produced widespread increases in vortex-space effective connectivity and reduced network modularity, whereas escitalopram showed no comparable changes. Despite these differences, greater increases in brain turbulence (i.e., spatiotemporal variability in local synchronisation) were associated with greater symptom reduction in both treatments, with a significant post-treatment increase in responders. These findings suggest that psilocybin and escitalopram may reorganise brain dynamics in markedly different ways and yet share dynamical features associated with clinical improvement. Overall, vortex-space modelling offers a promising framework for characterising brain dynamics in depression and its successful treatment.

papers.title: Data-Driven Decomposition of Precisely Aligned Fiber-Orientation-Preserving Probabilistic Tractography Connectomes with Non-Negative Matrix Factorization
papers.abstract: The major goals of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) were to characterize the structural and functional connectivity of the human brain. Although there has been tremendous work done for functional connectivity, including application of a variety of data driven decomposition approaches, structural connectivity from the HCP has seen less attention. This work presents a collection of methodological advances that, in combination, enable similar approaches to be applied to diffusion tractography data. Here, we use multi-modal non-linear volumetric alignment with FSL's MultiMOdal Registration Framework (MMORF) to precisely align white matter tracts and globular gray matter nuclei, use the White matter Hierarchical Modelling (WHIM) method to align voxel-wise fiber orientations, enable efficient GPU-accelerated computation and storage of full resolution probabilistic gray matter x white matter x fiber sparse tractography matrices in precise alignment across individuals using the aforementioned MMORF and WHIM alignments together with areal-feature-based cortical surface registration. These tractography dense connectomes can be averaged across individuals and sparse, computationally efficient non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) can be applied to perform data-driven decompositions into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories. The primary outputs of this effort to date are 1) A set of HCP software pipelines enabling such analyses, 2) A new unbiased HCP-derived volumetric standard space that is representative of the young adult brain and follows ACPC orientation conventions across individuals. 3) Reproducible NMF decompositions of HCP young adult tractography data into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories, which could be projected using non-negative dual regression back to individuals. These data represent a starting point for a new generation of data-driven atlasing efforts for human white matter, and these methods can be applied to study the white matter in development, aging, and brain diseases.

papers.title: ASTEROID, A Validated Annotated Dataset of Analytical Decisions in Graph Theory Based fMRI
papers.abstract: Graph theory-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies use complex analytical pipelines, but methodological decisions are often reported in unstructured text, limiting systematic comparison and the design of multiverse analyses. Here, we describe ASTEROID, a structured annotation dataset derived from 156 graph theory-based human fMRI study publications. Its schema contains 125 labels, comprising 61 methodological labels and 64 labels for study characteristics and experimental design. An LLM-assisted workflow generated initial annotations, which underwent automated quality-control checks and expert human review. The dataset captures preprocessing, functional connectivity, and graph-analysis decisions. Within these categories, steps and their sequence, software, algorithms, parameters, and supporting text spans are included where available. This accompanying paper provides prompt specifications, processing scripts, and documentation, and describes an interactive viewer that supports exploration of the annotation schema and the study records. ASTEROID enables comparison of reported analytical choices, the informed design of multiverse-based robustness analysis and supports the development and evaluation of automated methodological information-extraction tools and educational resources for fMRI data analysis.

papers.title: Prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling promotes maladaptive plasticity of direct pathway striatal projection neurons
papers.abstract: As Parkinson's disease (PD) progresses and nigrostriatal dopamine (DA) neuron degeneration worsens, DA replacement therapies shift from restoring motor function to evoking dyskinesia. How disease progression mediates this transition remains poorly understood. Here, we optimized a 6-hydroxydopamine (6OHDA) model that reliably generates multiple severities of DA axon denervation within the striatum of individual mice. We identify a critical denervation threshold at which direct-pathway striatal projection neurons (dSPNs), which are key drivers of dyskinesia become pathologically hyperresponsive to DA. Using slice electrophysiology, we establish that denervation-induced increase in intrinsic excitability is insufficient to explain the aberrant response of dSPNs to DA. We further demonstrate using genetic and chemogenetic manipulations that prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling drives the pathological transformation of dSPNs cell-autonomously, and that sustained Gs-coupled metabotropic receptor signaling in dSPNs is sufficient to both prevent and reverse it. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how PD progression renders striatal circuits vulnerable to DA-evoked motor complications and identify sustained signaling by Gs-coupled receptors as a potential avenue for preventing or reversing denervation-induced maladaptive striatal plasticity.

papers.title: Preprocessing Determines Whether Fractal Biomarkers Detect Neurodegeneration: A Systematic Evaluation Across Five fMRI Pipelines
papers.abstract: Fractal analysis of resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has been proposed for detecting altered neural dynamics in Alzheimers disease (AD), but the effect of preprocessing on these measurements is poorly constrained. We evaluated 229 ADNI3 participants (156 cognitively normal [CN], 60 mild cognitive impairment [MCI], and 13 AD) processed with five ENIGMA HALFpipe variants. Each scan contained 197 volumes (TR = 3.0 s) and 434 regional time series. The reported CN-AD effect varied 4.5-fold for the detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) Hurst exponent and 13.1-fold for Sample Entropy; both measures met p < 0.05 only after aCompCor. Under aCompCor, mean H was 0.812 in CN, 0.827 in MCI, and 0.872 in AD (d = -1.40, p = 0.0003), whereas the other four DFA effects were approximately d = -0.31 to -0.40. A variance decomposition attributed 41.5% of total H variance to pipeline, 44.5% to participant, and 0.3% to diagnosis. Whole-brain analysis found higher H in AD across 16 of 18 networks, with 36 cortical regions surviving false-discovery-rate correction. Synthetic fractional Gaussian noise experiments confirmed monotonic DFA estimation at the available scan length. The small AD group makes all disease-effect estimates exploratory. These results show that preprocessing choice can determine whether fractal group differences are detectable and should therefore be treated as part of the biomarker definition.

papers.title: Common organization of collective dynamics across divergent self-organized neural architectures
papers.abstract: Brain organoids and other model neuronal networks build synaptic circuits through self-organization, and different protocols yield markedly different architectures, letting us test how collective dynamics depend on large-scale organization. We compared organoids of layered cortical-like structure against networks of cell-body clusters joined by axonal cables, quantifying the reproducible patterns of population activity in each. Bursts occurred in both architectures and comprised several collective patterns in each, so no single recurring template describes them. Recurrent activation sequences capture only part of this organization, sequence participation is graded, and neurons that rarely join a sequence still contribute to the shared dynamics. The patterns also pick out overlapping neuronal groups with propagation-like spatial order. Although the patterns differed between tissue models, their organization was conserved, and remained unchanged under pharmacological increases in network activity. Recurrent sequences therefore represent one manifestation of a broader collective organization that emerges across distinct self-organized neural architectures.

papers.title: Expanded representation and function of PDF neurons in the mosquito circadian network
papers.abstract: Female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes can transmit pathogens when they bite humans, their preferred hosts, and this host-seeking drive is tightly gated by time of day. Daily rhythms depend on the molecular clock and communication among clock neurons, yet mosquito circadian network organization remains poorly understood. Using a mosquito-specific PERIOD antibody, we mapped the putative clock network of Aedes aegypti and found that neurons expressing the neuropeptide Pigment-Dispersing Factor (PDF) make up a much larger proportion of clock neurons compared to other insects, indicating a divergent network organization. PDF neurons are required for normal rhythms across insects, but whether their importance scales with their abundance in the network is unknown. We therefore tested the functional role of this expanded PDF neuron population in mosquitoes: we show that electrically silencing Aedes aegypti PDF neurons abolished the separation of daily activity into morning and evening peaks and led to misaligned clock protein rhythms across circadian neurons, even under entraining light-dark cycles. Thus, in a network built around an unusually large PDF population, PDF neuron activity plays an outsized role in behavioral timing and network synchrony.

papers.title: Rage bait: a neurofunctional signature of moral outrage elicited by social media
papers.abstract: Moral outrage is ubiquitous online, with powerful emotional and motivational consequences for social life. Combining naturalistic fMRI during exposure to short-form social-media videos depicting moral violations with predictive modeling, we developed a neurofunctional signature of subjective moral outrage (MONS) in discovery/validation (n=80/30) cohorts. MONS predicted experienced outrage and punishment tendencies across cohorts. Positive predictive weights encompassed regions implicated in mentalizing, threat detection and action initiation (precuneus, posterior cingulate, periaqueductal gray, hypothalamus, cerebellum), whereas negative weights involved valuation and behavioral flexibility systems (amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex). Across 11 datasets (n=478), MONS captured anger and disgust but was dissociable from general negative affect and affective arousal. Notably, MONS did not predict perceived moral wrongness in conventional moral judgment paradigms, suggesting that moral outrage is not reducible to more cognitive moral evaluation. Findings provide a moral outrage neurofunctional model that delineates its relationship to other affective states and distinguishes it from traditional moral judgment.

papers.title: Sex-dependent gating of astrocyte-driven nociceptive plasticity
papers.abstract: Sex differences in pain are well established, yet how nociceptive processing is differentially regulated across sexes remains poorly understood. Here, we show that spinal astrocytes provide pathway-specific control of acute nociceptive synaptic plasticity in rats. Chemogenetic activation of distinct astrocytic G-protein-coupled receptor pathways induced synaptic depression or potentiation at spinal nociceptive synapses in males, but failed to evoke detectable plasticity in females. Despite this lack of astrocyte-induced synaptic plasticity, females developed mechanical hypersensitivity comparable to males, revealing a dissociation between synaptic plasticity and pain-related behavior. Gonadectomy prevented astrocyte-induced plasticity in males, whereas testosterone treatment enabled Gq-dependent synaptic depression in ovariectomized females. Females exhibited more prominent perineuronal net labeling, and enzymatic degradation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components enabled Gq-dependent synaptic depression in females. Together, these findings identify hormonal status and ECM organization as important determinants of the susceptibility of spinal nociceptive circuits to astrocyte-driven synaptic plasticity.

papers.title: Adaptive behaviors emerge from Hebbian-like plasticity through flexible attractors
papers.abstract: Adaptive behavior is commonly framed as an optimization problem, in which organisms learn to maximize reward. Here we show that simple networks with local, Hebbian-like learning rules, which have no reward objective, nonetheless reproduce hallmark features of animal reward-seeking when placed in closed-loop environments where rewards arrive as ordinary sensory input. Six canonical local learning rules were tested under these conditions, and despite most rules being designed for unsupervised representation learning, all rules learned to seek out signal. However, at the parameters tested, only one rule, prospective configuration, robustly captured all of a set of tested phenomena: reward-magnitude-dependent learning rates, probability matching, memory retention across contexts, and switching between exploration and exploitation with heavy-tailed statistics. In these networks, actions that produce input become self-sustaining states (attractors) of network dynamics. Attractors reside in an activity-weight space and mediate behaviors, and adapt to their environments rather than being fixed properties of the networks. These flexible geometries provide a parsimonious account of how heavy-tailed runs of repeated choices, which resemble Levy flights seen in foraging, also change with the environment. A single framework then makes predictions about behavior and neural population geometries that can be used to investigate the learning dynamics of the brain.

papers.title: Temporal regularity shapes thalamocortical responses and deviance sensitivity in the anesthetized rat
papers.abstract: The brain uses regularities in the sensory environment to anticipate upcoming events, but whether predictions about stimulus identity and timing rely on dissociable neural mechanisms remains unclear. Here, we independently manipulated the temporal structure of acoustic sequences (rhythmic vs. jittered) and stimulus deviance of sequence elements (deviants vs. standards) while recording local field potentials (LFPs) and multiunit activity (AMUA) simultaneously from ventral and dorsal medial geniculate body (MGB) and cortical layers in 9 female anesthetized rats. Temporal structure robustly modulated neural responses throughout the auditory thalamocortical system. LFP responses were stronger for jittered than rhythmic stimulation across all layers of both primary and non-primary auditory cortex, with effects spanning early and later poststimulus intervals. AMUA responses showed a complementary temporal-predictability effect in both dorsal and ventral MGB, with stronger responses to jittered than rhythmic stimuli. In contrast, stimulus deviance effects were strongly dependent on temporal context and recording site. Deviant standard differences were enhanced under jittered stimulation in cortex and in early MGB responses, whereas later MGB responses showed a context dependent reversal. Finally, AMUA based Granger analyses revealed sustained jitter specific directed influences from both dorsal and ventral MGB toward multiple cortical layers during the poststimulus period. Together, these findings demonstrate that temporal regularity robustly modulates auditory thalamocortical responses and is associated with changes in directed interactions between thalamus and cortex. Responses to stimulus deviance, in turn, depend on temporal context and recording site. These findings reveal distinct but interacting neural signatures of temporal regularity and stimulus deviance in the auditory thalamocortical system.

papers.title: Historeceptomics Profiling of Ketamine
papers.abstract: Ketamine elicits distinctive neuropsychiatric phenotypes from a complex and as yet elusive mechanism of action. Here, we applied an updated Historeceptomics approach to identify molecular targets and brain tissues that may contribute to its antidepressant, analgesic, and dissociative effects. Historeceptomics generates multidimensional target-tissue fingerprints by integrating drug-target activity with tissue-specific target expression, providing an anatomic profile of drug action. The results suggest that ketamine activity on NMDA receptors in the prefrontal and cingulate cortices and the amygdala may contribute to ketamine improvements in social functioning for MDD. However, this same receptor-tissue activity may invoke hallucinatory effects at higher intensity or with engagement of additional brain regions. The central nervous system (CNS) fingerprint for ketamine was compared with those of other psychoactive drugs, showing overlap with fingerprints from other antidepressant, hallucinogenic, and analgesic drugs. Some ketamine effects may be traced to specific enantiomers or metabolites of ketamine. These findings provide new insights into the mechanisms by which ketamine elicits its unique phenotype and demonstrate the utility of using Historeceptomics to understand complex drug action.

papers.title: Testing hypothesized neural substrates with lesions
papers.abstract: Correlative neuroimaging generates anatomical hypotheses causally testable by lesion studies. Regionally weighted lesion volume-deficit regression - comparing slopes of behavioural dependence on damage inside vs outside a hypothesized neural substrate - and compartmental volume comparisons inheriting the same logic have been widely employed for this task, but without analytical examination or empirical validation of the underlying methodology. Here we show analytically that this approach does not provide a valid test of whether the hypothesized compartment identifies the true substrate. To illustrate the empirical consequences, we conduct semi-synthetic simulations using 4119 ischaemic lesions, modelling behavioural deficits dependent on a global lesion attribute, on widely investigated distributed cortical networks and white matter tracts, or on a right frontal substrate of fluid intelligence previously identified by multivariate methods. We apply regionally weighted regression with each hypothesized compartment as the target over 5000 iterations spanning multiple realistic noise levels. Where the hypothesized target is not the true substrate, we find spuriously significant dependence despite definitionally absent anatomical specificity; adjustment for lesion volume attenuates or exacerbates the observed bias dependent on the chosen target. Conversely, where the target is the true substrate, lesion volume correction universally reduces already poor sensitivity. Our analysis potentially explains common discrepancies across localisation studies, and highlights the necessity of multivariate approaches that explicitly model lesion and substrate anatomy at finely resolved spatial scales.

papers.title: AAV-Mediated Astrogliosis Recapitulates Early Neuroinflammatory and Bioenergetic Features of Alzheimer''s Disease in Mice
papers.abstract: Neuroinflammation and altered neuron-astrocyte metabolic interactions are increasingly recognized as early features of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, the underlying metabolic adaptations remain incompletely understood. This study employed deuterium magnetic resonance spectroscopy (DMRS) following administration of deuterium labeled glucose and acetate to investigate neuronal and astroglial substrate utilization and metabolic fluxes, respectively, in adenovirus-induced neuroinflammation and early-stage APPNL-F/NL-F mice. In adenovirus-induced astrogliosis, increased acetate derived [4,4'-2H2]Glx (d2-Glx) production suggested enhanced astrocytic acetate utilization and TCA cycle activity. Conversely, reduced glucose derived d2-Glx despite comparable glucose uptake suggested a diminished neuronal activity due to potentially impaired neuronal oxidative metabolism. However, the glucose-derived lactate labeling remained unchanged, suggesting differential effects on oxidative and non-oxidative pathways of glucose metabolism. Similarly, 3-month-old APPNL-F/NL-F mice exhibited significantly increased [2,2',2''-2H3]acetate (d3-Ace) influx compared with wild-type controls, suggesting early alterations in astrocytic substrate utilization. While glucose uptake remained unchanged, glucose derived Glx and lactate showed modest, non-significant decreases, potentially reflecting early alterations in glucose metabolism. Overall, both models exhibited a metabolic pattern characterized by increased astrocytic acetate utilization with trends towards reduced glucose associated metabolism, with more pronounced changes in adenovirus-induced astrogliosis. These findings highlight the utility of DMRS for investigating dynamic metabolic adaptations during neuroinflammation and early AD pathogenesis. Importantly, the adenovirus-induced astrogliosis model recapitulates key metabolic alterations associated with the neuroinflammatory aspects of AD. As such, it provides a valuable complementary platform for investigating mechanisms driving early metabolic dysfunction and evaluating therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring neuron-astrocyte metabolic interactions prior to the onset of substantial neurodegeneration.

papers.title: fMRI hyperscanning reveals that coordinated exploration predicts successful conversation
papers.abstract: Conversations among friends are often more dynamic, enjoyable, and wide-ranging than those between strangers. How do friends do this? We propose that inside jokes, shared experiences, and mutual interests give friends an aligned mental map, allowing them to leap between topics without losing each other. Strangers may begin in separate mental landscapes, limiting opportunities for exploration as they take smaller steps to avoid confusion. To test these possibilities, we tracked the dyadic dynamics of friends (n = 60) and strangers (n = 54) as they engaged in a real-time conversation using fMRI hyperscanning. We employed Hyper-Hidden-Markov-Modeling to project partner's neural states into a shared latent space and to segment them into discrete events. This allowed us to quantify how similarly each dyad represented each event (representational alignment), and how spread out conversational events were in latent space (representational exploration). We tested how neural alignment predicted exploration, how both neural measures relate to the breadth of topics discussed, and how they predicted the subjective experience of the conversation quality in friends and strangers. We found that the more a dyad aligned neurally, the more they also explored. While both neural alignment and exploration predicted the breadth of conversations, only neural exploration predicted better perceived conversation quality. Friends were more neurally aligned, which was associated with more exploration. Thus, when friends brains represent the world more similarly to each other, they tend to embark on more diverse and far-reaching conversations spanning a broader range of topics, all while staying anchored in common ground.

papers.title: The information architecture of the naturalistic human brain
papers.abstract: How does the brain orchestrate its central currency, information, for complex adaptive cognition in the real world? Here we provide a comprehensive investigation into the spatiotemporal structure of qualitatively distinct modes of information dynamics in the human brain under ecological conditions. Applying a novel framework for information decomposition to fMRI data from individuals watching full-length feature films, we reveal a multidimensional large-scale information architecture, wherein different schemes for storing, transferring, and transforming representations occupy disjoint topographic and network profiles. Further, this architecture reveals a computational division of labour, with certain regions acting as generalists that support multiple information-processing schemes and others specialising in a few. We show how these interactions reconfigure over time, coalescing into a structured cycle synchronised by sensory input, whose elements are tuned to semantic kinematics. Finally, we replicate these findings in an independent, large-scale dataset. Together, we provide a formal and empirical foundation for understanding the principles that govern distributed computation in the human brain during everyday life.

papers.title: Sensory Change Detection Unfolds Within a Shared Low-Dimensional Brain-State Landscape
papers.abstract: Detecting behaviorally relevant sensory changes requires the coordination of modality-specific sensory processing with shared attentional and control systems, yet how these processes are organized and evolve across large-scale brain networks remains unclear. Here, we investigated the connectivity architecture and temporal dynamics of auditory and visual target detection using fMRI acquired during matched oddball tasks. Cross-modal partial least-squares analysis revealed a low dimensional architecture comprising two dominant, modality-general dimensions and additional modality-biased components. The shared dimensions distinguished a sensory attention action configuration from a higher order associative and contextual configuration, whereas modality biased dimensions showed distinct organization involving frontoparietal and attentional networks. Projecting these connectivity patterns onto time-resolved BOLD activity revealed a common dominant latent space with graded regions of preferential occupancy across modalities. Overlap-adjusted event-related analyses further showed that auditory and visual targets were associated with a similar initial displacement along the first temporal latent dimension, followed by modality-dependent trajectories, particularly along the second dimension. This later divergence reflected different balances of regional contributions within a largely shared cortical architecture. By integrating dimensionality reduction of high dimensional functional connectivity with network and temporal analyses, our findings link the spatial organization of distributed cortical systems to their evolving responses, revealing how shared brain networks can support both common and modality-dependent aspects of sensory target detection.

papers.title: Pharmacological co-targeting of Hippo and Wnt pathways induces robust Muller glia proliferation and reprogramming in the adult mouse retina
papers.abstract: Reprogramming of endogenous Muller glia (MG) into functional neurons represents a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of irreversible retinal blinding diseases. In adult mammals, however, insufficient MG proliferation constitutes a primary bottleneck that restricts successful MG reprogramming and impairs retinal structural and functional restoration. Here, we demonstrated that simultaneous chemical inhibition of Hippo signaling with TRULI and activation of Wnt signaling with CHIR-99021 elicited robust proliferation of endogenous MG in the adult mouse retinal explants. Following combinatorial drug treatment, MG exhibited gradual induction of the retinal progenitor marker PAX6 and the bipolar/photoreceptor lineage determinant Otx2, without concomitant elevation of the fibrotic marker GFAP, supporting the initiation of MG reprogramming. Mechanistically, our findings revealed that YAP and {beta}-catenin might act cooperatively to induce the expression of MYC, a core transcription factor governing cell cycle progression and somatic cell reprogramming. Elevated MYC accumulation in MG transcriptionally activated Cyclin D1 expression, which, together with the downregulation of the cell cycle inhibitor p27Kip1, drove efficient MG cell cycle re-entry and proliferation. Collectively, this study establishes a pure chemical combinatorial strategy to trigger robust proliferation and initiate reprogramming of adult mammalian MG. Our findings provide a feasible alternative approach to promote retinal regeneration and lay a foundation for the future clinical treatment of degenerative retinal diseases.

papers.title: NeuroImgAgent: a multi-agent platform for cross-species fMRI analysis with evidence-gated quality control
papers.abstract: Cross-species functional MRI analysis requires coordinating specialized workflows and assessing intermediate outputs. We present NeuroImgAgent, a multi-agent platform driven by large language models that translates natural-language requests into workflows for humans, macaques, rats and mice. Quantitative checks and vision-language model assessments determine whether processing continues, enters bounded recovery or stops. Across 268 paired cases, preprocessing metrics were broadly comparable to those of fMRIPrep, AFNI and RABIES. With GPT-5.5, NeuroImgAgent corrected 111 of 120 induced orientation errors and passed all 52 intent-recognition and planning tasks, 8 of 9 recovery tasks and 11 of 14 tool-construction tasks on NeuroAgentBench. In 120 paired challenge cases, the full configuration increased usability from 76.7% to 92.5%, as assessed by blinded experts, and reduced unusable outputs delivered without warning from 18.3% to 4.2% of cases relative to quality-control ablation.

papers.title: Constructing value on the fly from episodic memory supports flexible decision-making
papers.abstract: Value-based decisions often require people to flexibly draw on and combine information from past experiences to evaluate novel stimuli and adapt to changing demands. Although numerous studies have highlighted the involvement of episodic memory in value-based decision-making, whether and how a common episodic mechanism can support diverse decision-making scenarios remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce GENESIS-Value, a computational framework that constructs value on the fly by retrieving and integrating episodic memories, rather than relying on stable, precomputed value representations. The model combines generative stimulus representations with a flexible query-key-value retrieval mechanism, allowing the same memory store to support different valuation and choice strategies. Across five simulations, we demonstrate that GENESIS-Value can use episodic sampling to reconstruct the values of experienced stimuli, generalize to novel stimuli based on shared features, estimate feature values, guide both individual and sequential choices, and select among multiple offers involving different rewards and levels of risk. We further show that retrieval can be guided by stimulus features, temporal proximity, reminders, and reward outcomes, as well as combinations of these factors, enabling adaptation to different decision demands without requiring separate value functions. The model also captures qualitative behavioral signatures reported in empirical studies of episodic decision-making. Together, these findings establish a unified computational account of how episodic retrieval can support diverse forms of value-based inference and choice. Rather than replacing stable value representations, episodic retrieval may provide a complementary mechanism that allows decision-makers to flexibly address a variety of choice scenarios by reconstructing the value of available options on the fly.

papers.title: Targeting Heparan Sulfate 3-O-Sulfation Enhances Acetylcholine Receptor Clustering and Stabilizes Neuromuscular Junctions in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
papers.abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a severe neuromuscular disease caused by dystrophin deficiency, leading to progressive muscle degeneration and neuromuscular junction (NMJ) instability. Using rat models of DMD, we identified a dysregulation in heparan sulfate (HS) biosynthesis at the NMJ, characterized by reduced expression of Hs6st2 and Hs3st5 genes that encode sulfotransferases required for the production of rare 3-O-sulfated heparan sulfate (3S-HS) forms. These genes act synergistically to enhance agrin signaling: their co-expression in myotubes potentiates acetylcholine receptor clustering, and HSPG mimics bearing tetrasulfated 3-O-sulfated motifs reproduce this effect and promote Agrin-LRP4 interaction. In DMD rats, muscle co-transduction of Hs6st2 and Hs3st5 prevents NMJ fragmentation and improves muscle strength. These findings identify 3S-HSs as novel regulators of NMJ stability and support HS modulation as a complementary therapeutic strategy in DMD.

papers.title: The mechanical nature of injury shapes the composition and temporal dynamics of inflammation after traumatic spinal cord injury
papers.abstract: The pathophysiology of traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) is a complex, evolving process that begins with a mechanical trauma. Progressive secondary damage then occurs, in which neuroinflammation plays a pivotal role. Much has been learned about the persistent inflammatory response during the chronic phase of SCI. However, variations in lesion models, animal species, strains, and the post-lesion intervals investigated make it difficult to conclude on how inflammation contributes to recovery or to exacerbation of damage. Here, we systematically compared two preclinical rat models of thoracic SCI: contusion and bilateral dorsal hemisection (bDH), that produce severe injuries leading to comparable initial locomotor deficits. We present a detailed analysis of neuroinflammatory temporal dynamics from acute (1-7 days), subacute (14 days), and chronic stages (> 4 weeks). The two models shared some inflammatory patterns, but specific cellular and molecular responses differed in magnitude, composition, and temporal evolution. These signature inflammatory dynamics were associated with differences in endogenous axonal plasticity, astroglial remodeling and progressive lesion maturation, and with distinct functional recovery rates. As the lesion gradually became chronic, inflammatory activity was remodeled, but persisted. These results reveal the interplay between the mechanical cause of SCI, the corresponding immune response, and the ensuing tissue remodeling processes. They highlight the importance of injury context and subsequent evolution. We discuss them as contributions to our understanding of the physiopathology of spinal cord lesions, with the broader goal of designing therapeutic strategies aiming to appropriately modulate inflammation

papers.title: Dissociated network and cellular remodeling in the hippocampal-cortical circuit after induction of neuronal hyperexcitability
papers.abstract: Neuronal hyperexcitability (NHE) can leave lasting consequences in neuronal circuits. It is often assumed that hyperexcitable neurons give rise to hyperactive networks. Here we asked how a single injection of kainic acid, which induces NHE without seizures, reshapes the hippocampal-cortical circuit at the cellular and network levels two months later. Using high-density microelectrode arrays in acute slices, we found a long-lasting reduction in spontaneous firing and bursting across the hippocampal regions, a lower proportion of active electrodes throughout the circuit, and weaker coupling from CA1 to the entorhinal cortex. In contrast, whole-cell recordings revealed region- and cell-type-specific changes in intrinsic excitability. CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons and CA3 interneurons exhibited increased evoked firing, whereas CA1 interneurons exhibited reduced evoked firing. Deep-layer entorhinal neurons, however, received less excitatory synaptic input and fired less. Thus, network and cellular alterations were dissociated after NHE. Finally, a pharmacological challenge with the GluK1 agonist ATPA revealed region-specific changes in network responsiveness, with a blunted response in CA3 and enhanced response in the non-entorhinal cortex, with no differences in DG, CA1 or entorhinal cortex. These findings suggest that, after the induction of NHE, region- and cell-type-specific neuronal remodeling coexists with reduced network activity ex vivo, and that the state of the circuit cannot be inferred from the properties of its individual neurons.

papers.title: Early life stress reduces prefrontal dendritic spine density in adult male mice
papers.abstract: Early life stress (ELS) is a major risk factor for anxiety, depression and substance use disorders later in life, and it is thought to act in part by changing how emotion-regulating circuits develop. The prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) cortices exert top-down control over the basolateral amygdala (BLA), and this circuit is still maturing during early postnatal life. Stress in adulthood removes dendritic spines from prefrontal neurons, but it is less clear whether ELS causes lasting spine changes across this circuit, and the IL in particular has rarely been studied. Here, we asked whether ELS alters dendritic spine density in the PL, IL and BLA of adult male mice. From postnatal day (PND) 10 to 17, ELS pups were separated from the dam for 3 h per day and individually isolated from their littermates, and their home cage had reduced nesting material until PND21. Control pups were separated together with their littermates for only 15 min per day and kept standard nesting. In adulthood, brains were processed for Golgi-Cox staining, and spines were counted on proximal apical and basal dendrites of layer II/III pyramidal neurons in the PL and IL, and on dendrites of principal neurons in the BLA. ELS reduced spine density by approximately 30% in the IL and PL dendrites, with the largest losses concentrated on proximal apical dendrites. The BLA showed a smaller reduction of about 12%. These preliminary findings suggest that ELS leads to an important and lasting loss of dendritic spines in prefrontal regions that regulate emotional responses.

papers.title: Tonic dopamine regulates cell-type-specific PKA activity and motivated behavior
papers.abstract: Dopamine in the striatum fluctuates on fast ``phasic`` and slow ``tonic`` timescales. Although disruptions in tonic dopamine have been implicated in the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disease, the effect of slow, minutes-long fluctuations in dopamine on neuronal activity and behavior remain unknown. Here we use two-color fluorescence lifetime photometry at high temporal resolution (FLIPR) and calibrated optogenetic and chemogenetic manipulations to determine the impact of tonic dopamine on motivated behavior and downstream signaling in vivo. We establish a method for tracking tonic dopamine using FLIPR and determine that dopamine release fluctuates across short (100s of milliseconds) and long (10s of minutes) timescales. We find that dopamine type 1 (D1R) and type 2 (D2R) receptor expressing spiny projection neurons (SPNs) are differentially affected by changes in tonic dopamine in vivo, confirming long-standing hypothesis on tonic dopamine function in the striatum. Finally, we show that accumbal tonic dopamine levels predict and causally mediate an animal`s motivation to work for reward by regulating the rate of reward-motivated actions and engagement in a progressive ratio task. Altogether, we show that tonic dopamine affects downstream signaling and motivated behavior, and establish a new set of methods that allows for careful capture and manipulation of tonic dopamine in vivo.

papers.title: Semaglutide quiets "food noise" in mice by impairing the wanting, but not the liking, of glucose
papers.abstract: Semaglutide and other GLP-1 receptor agonists are transforming obesity treatment, and patients often describe a quieting of intrusive food thoughts that motivate overconsumption of ultra-palatable foods, referred to as "food noise," yet it remains unclear which components of feeding behavior they act upon. Here, we designed a battery of behavioral tasks that separate the perceptual, hedonic, and motivational components of glucose intake in mice. Semaglutide impaired sweet taste categorization (in a psychophysical task) and induced conditioned taste avoidance not aversion, and thus left palatability intact. Its largest effect, however, was on motivation: it selectively disrupted the active pursuit of glucose and, to a lesser extent, lipids, sparing passive intake. In a novel lick-triggered taste alternation task, two fixed sippers delivered either glucose or a second tastant (e.g., saccharin or lipids), with the tastants swapping positions after a set number of licks. This design separated effortless consumption, when the swap brought glucose directly to the mouse (passive hit), from effortful pursuit requiring crossing to the opposite sipper (active hit). A single dose of semaglutide left passive hits intact, but markedly reduced active hits: mice readily exploited glucose that came to them, yet often failed to go after it. As the drug's effect waned, mice regained body weight by selectively overconsuming standard chow over glucose, and glucose over lipids, a shift in diet choice that persisted through the end of the experiment. Thus, semaglutide impairs the wanting, but not the liking, of glucose, providing (in mice) a behavioral correlate of the quieting of "food noise" reported by patients.

papers.title: Investigating the effect of acute consumption of kiwifruit on cognitive function using functional MRI
papers.abstract: Objectives: Acute nutritional interventions may modulate cognitive function and underlying brain activity. This study investigated the impact of consuming three kiwifruit varieties - green (Zespri Green), gold (Zespri SunGold), and red (Zespri RubyRed) - on cognitive performance and brain activation using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Methods: Fourteen healthy participants completed a randomized, repeated-measures study involving four MRI sessions following consumption of each kiwifruit type and a maltodextrin control. Cognitive function was assessed using an N-back working memory task during fMRI acquisition. Behavioural performance, psychometric measures (mood, fatigue, appetite), and blood biomarkers (vitamin C) were also collected. Results: Kiwifruit consumption significantly increased plasma vitamin C levels relative to control, with peak concentrations observed at 100 minutes post-consumption. Behaviourally, task difficulty increased with N-back load, while psychometric measures indicated greater positive affect following kiwifruit compared to control. fMRI results showed that the maltodextrin condition elicited broader brain activation, suggesting reduced neural efficiency. In contrast, kiwifruit -particularly the red variety - showed enhanced differentiation between low and high cognitive load (2-back vs. 0-back), with increased activation in regions associated with working memory and cognitive control. Conclusions: These findings suggest that acute kiwifruit consumption may enhance cognitive efficiency and modulate brain responses, with effects varying by kiwifruit cultivar.

papers.title: Zhx2 expression in the mouse brain
papers.abstract: Prescription opioids like oxycodone (OXY; the active component in OxyContin) continue to drive the ongoing opioid use disorder (OUD) epidemic due to their widespread prescription and distribution. Genetic factors influencing pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of opioids can have profound impacts on drug response and, in turn, influence risk for OUD. We previously used quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping and gene validation to identify zinc-finger homeobox 2 (Zhx2) loss-of-function as a quantitative trait gene and mechanism underlying increased brain concentration of oxymorphone (OMOR) following systemic administration of OXY in BALB/cJ females that was linked to increased OXY reward. To test whether we could rescue the behavioral phenotype, we overexpressed Zhx2 in the brain via retro-orbital injection of a brain-specific adeno-associated virus (AAV). We observed restricted Zhx2 expression (especially females), with more widespread expression in males. Consequently, we did not observe any significant effect of brain Zhx2 overexpression on OXY reward as measured via conditioned place preference (CPP). However, Zhx2 overexpression did protect against OXY-induced weight loss in females following a high-dose OXY regimen. Despite the effect on weight loss, Zhx2 overexpression had no effect on spontaneous or naloxone-precipitated withdrawal behaviors. We then examined native Zhx2 protein expression in the brains of the BALB/cByJ substrain (showing wild-type levels of Zhx2 expression) via immunohistochemical co-localization and found that Zhx2 is mainly expressed in neurons located in key reward, motivational, and emotion-related regions such as the hippocampus (HPC), amygdala, striatum (Str), and cerebellum. To summarize, Zhx2 overexpression via retro-orbital AAV administration was quite limited, yet had significant effects on opioid-induced weight loss. Furthermore, for the first time, we provide anatomical visualization of Zhx2 expression at the protein level in neurons vs. glia throughout multiple brain regions.

papers.title: Dissociable patterns of neurophysiological alterations during guided search in schizophrenia and autism: Evidence from fixation-related potentials, alpha modulation, and functional MRI.
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia (SZ) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are associated with convergent differences in social perception relative to non-autistic, non-schizophrenia controls (NC), but divergent patterns of alterations in early visual activity. Here, we used multimodal imaging during the Guided Visual Search task to investigate the differential patterns of early visual alteration across SZ and ASD including superior colliculus (SC) and pulvinar nucleus. In Experiment 1, simultaneous eye tracking and EEG were obtained from 91 individuals (35 NC, 20 ASD, 36 SZ). Fixation-related potential (FRP) was time-locked to fixation onset. In Experiment 2, fMRI during Guided Search was obtained from a partly overlapping sample of 71 individuals (27 NC, 25 ASD, 19 SZ). In behavioral analyses, SZ was associated with significantly prolonged search time (d=.74, p=.003), which was attributable primarily to reduced mean saccade amplitude, whereas ASD was associated with a small advantage (d=.35), which was not statistically significant. In EEG analyses, SZ was associated with reduced amplitude of the FRP P1 (lambda) response (d=1.15, p<.0001) relative to NC that remained significant following control for saccade size (p<.0001), but with normal task-related modulation of background alpha activity. In contrast, ASD was associated with normal FRP amplitude and larger alpha suppression (d=.83, p=.007) that was attributable to increased alpha levels during pre-task fixation (at matched pre-onset alpha levels, d=.14, p=.66). Within SZ, P1 correlated with the MCCB composite (r=.56, p=.001). Within ASD, ADOS-2 Communication correlated with P1 (r=.51, p=.024) and with the broadband change from pre-onset to search (r=-.51, p=.030). In fMRI, SZ was associated with correlated activation reductions in the Visual1 (Sidak p<.001) and Visual2 (Sidak p=.022) networks and SC (Sidak p=.019), whereas activation was unaffected in the Dorsal Attention and Frontoparietal networks, Frontal Eye Fields and pulvinar. In ASD, activation was increased in pulvinar (Sidak p[≤].038), but unaffected elsewhere. Cortical activation patterns associated with SC activation resembled those associated with P1 generation across groups. Overall, the findings support bottom-up disturbances of visual processing in schizophrenia. In autism, pre-onset alpha was higher and task-related suppression was larger.

papers.title: Unified CEBRA learns shared neural latents across recordings to map single-neuron contributions to population codes
papers.abstract: Neural computation is thought to rely on distributed populations; however, most single recording samples capture only a fraction of them, and rare cell types may contribute only a small proportion of neurons per session. Pooling many recordings could reveal how these populations encode information, but each recording samples different neurons, so their contributions cannot be easily compared directly. Here we show that recordings can be combined into a single model of all recorded neurons by aligning them with a shared label, used at both training and inference, placing every neuron's contribution to the population code on a common scale. This approach, called Unified CEBRA, retained interpretable task information across recordings in the monkey and mouse sensorimotor cortex, rat hippocampus, and mouse visual cortex. Pooling thousands of excitatory and inhibitory neurons from hundreds of sessions from mouse visual cortex, we found that the neurons that contributed most to the model's readout of visual features were not only the most strongly tuned, but also those that responded more reliably and were less coupled to co-recorded neurons. Unified CEBRA, therefore, can unveil coding principles studied at the population scale with mappable features to individual neurons from sparse, multi-session recordings using our new approach.
